title: When Weights Collide with Latents: Direct Weight-Space Arithmetic Induces Asymmetric Degeneration in Sparse Autoencoder Monosemanticity
domain: mechanistic interpretability (task-vector arithmetic vs sparse autoencoders)
tasks_benchmarks: SAE reconstruction MSE / cosine / L0 over 2,048 evaluation sequences
task vectors for Python code completion, GSM8k, toxicity filtering

headline_result.text: Scaling a task vector degrades SAE fidelity (reconstruction MSE rises from 0.268 at lambda 0 to 0.898 at lambda +2.0), subtraction hurts slightly more than addition (rho = 0.950), and a closed-form rotation (OLR-K) is claimed to recover up to 88.4% of dictionary alignment.
headline_result.quote: with an MSE of 0.26811. However, scaling to λ = +1.0 inflates the MSE to 0.45034 (+67.9% error), and scaling to λ = +2.0 causes an explosion to 0.89832 (+235.0% error).

key_claims.claim: Task-vector subtraction distorts SAE latents more than addition, with an asymmetry ratio of 0.950247 at |lambda| = 2.0.
key_claims.quote: This yields a verified asymmetry index of 0.950247. Task vector negation causes approximately 7.42% greater latent distortion than vector addition.

key_claims.claim: Primary latent retention drops below 50% once |lambda| reaches 1.0.
key_claims.quote: Primary latent retention drops below 50% at |λ| ≥ 1.0, proving that standard task arithmetic renders existing autoencoder dictionaries essentially obsolete for mechanistic monitoring.

key_claims.claim: Mid-network layers 6-9 are the most affected by weight arithmetic.
key_claims.quote: as signals enter the mid-network semantic processing zone (Layers 6-9), distortion peaks catastrophically (D7 = 0.94, D8 = 0.91).

key_claims.claim: A closed-form orthogonal re-projection (OLR-K) recovers most dictionary fidelity without retraining the SAE.
key_claims.quote: Within 15 iterations, OLR-K reduces reconstruction MSE from 0.450 to 0.284, recovering 88.4% of baseline dictionary fidelity.

key_claims.claim: The author frames 'weight-space programming' as linear task-vector arithmetic and attributes it to Takehi et al. (2024), not to LLM-driven editing.
key_claims.quote: Recently, Takehi et al. (2024 at MIT CSAIL) introduced Weight-Space Programming, establishing formal operators for composing model behaviors via linear arithmetic.

limitations_stated.text: OLR-K recovery falls to 60% or less when perturbations exceed |lambda| > 2.8.
limitations_stated.quote: These failure modes occur exclusively when task perturbations exceed |λ| > 2.8, where high-order non-linear terms dominate the Taylor expansion

notes_for_review: Not LLM-driven weight-space programming: it studies scalar task-vector arithmetic and its effect on sparse-autoencoder dictionaries, and mislabels this as WSP, citing a 'Takehi, Gu & Andreas (2024)' MIT preprint that does not match the 2026 MIT blog post. The document calls itself a 30-page monograph but has 19 pages, gives no code, data, task-vector construction details or seeds, and some numbers do not line up (e.g. abstract 'collapse by up to 74.2%' does not appear in the tables). Treat its numbers with caution; at most it is background on weight arithmetic and interpretability.
